text: Assumption 1 . (i) $p:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ and $q:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ are proper closed convex functions, and the proximal operator of $p$ and $q$ can be exactly evaluated. (ii) The set $\mathcal{Y}$ is bounded, namely, we have $\|y\|\leq D_{\mathbf{y}}$ for some $D_{\mathbf{y}}\geq 1$ . (iii) $h:\mathbb{R}^{m+n}\to\mathbb{R}$ is $L_{\nabla h}$ -smooth on $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}$ for some $L_{\nabla h}>0$ . For any $x\in\mathcal{X}$ , $h(x,\cdot)$ is concave on $\mathcal{Y}$ . (iv) Problem ( 1 ) has at least one optimal solution with finite optimal value $H^{*}=\min_{x}\max_{y}H(x,y)$ .

Definition 1 . For $\epsilon\geq 0$ , a point $(x,y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}$ is called an $\epsilon$ -stationary point of the minimax problem ( 1 ) if $\mathrm{dist}(0,\nabla_{x}h(x,y)+\partial p(x))\leq\epsilon,\qquad\mathrm{dist}(0,\nabla_{y}h(x,y)-\partial q(y))\leq\epsilon.$ We use the same definition for other composite minimax problems, with $h$ replaced by the corresponding smooth coupling.

Assumption 2 . The function $f$ is $\mu_{x}$ -strongly convex in $x$ , $\mu_{y}$ -strongly concave in $y$ , and $L_{\nabla f}$ -smooth on $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}$ , where $0<\mu_{y}\leq\mu_{x}\leq L_{\nabla f}$ .

Remark 1 . The ordering $\mu_{y}\leq\mu_{x}$ entails no loss of generality. If $\mu_{x}<\mu_{y}$ , exchanging the two variable blocks and reversing the objective sign yields the equivalent saddle-point with the curvature bounds and proximal mappings interchanged.

Assumption 3 . There exist an algorithm $\mathcal{A}(F,B,u^{0},L_{F},\mu)$ and constants $\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{A}}>0$ and $N_{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathbb{N}$ , with $N_{\mathcal{A}}\geq 1$ , such that the following holds. From any $u^{0}\in\dom B$ , one run of $\mathcal{A}$ generates, for every $\vartheta>0$ , a computed pair $(u,r)$ with $r\in(F+B)(u),\qquad\|r\|\leq\vartheta\|u^{0}-u^{*}\|,$ using at most $N_{\mathcal{A}}+\lceil\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{A}}L_{F}/\vartheta\rceil$ evaluations of $F$ and of the resolvent of $B$ , respectively. Every evaluation of $F$ is at a point of $\dom B$ . Both counts include initialization and computation of $r$ . The constants depend only on $\mathcal{A}$ , not on the inclusion, its parameters, or its initial point. Neither $u^{*}$ nor its distance from $u^{0}$ is an input.

Remark 2 . For the subdifferential operator $B$ used here, the EAG and past-EAG methods in [ 45 , Corollary 3.1] , with one forward–backward initialization step, satisfy Assumption 3 . With $\tau_{k}=1/(k+2)$ , one may take $(N_{\mathcal{A}},\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{A}})=(4,22)$ for EAG with stepsize $1/(2L_{F})$ , and $(N_{\mathcal{A}},\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{A}})=(4,28)$ for past-EAG with stepsize $1/(3L_{F})$ .

Remark 3 . It can be observed from ( 8 )–( 10 ) that $e^{k+1}$ is the original KKT residual, $\tilde{u}^{k+1}$ is an inexact proximal point for $\Phi$ , and $c^{k+1}$ is the next extrapolation center. Moreover, the inner test ( 7 ) controls the proximal inexactness, while ( 11 ) determines when the algorithm returns. The decreasing parameter $\gamma_{k}$ is used only in the initialization resolvent.

Remark 4 . The preliminary call determines $\lambda_{1}$ from the computed displacement. At each regularized iteration, $r^{k+1}$ is the residual of the regularized subproblem, and step 4 converts it to the original residual $e^{k+1}$ used in the stopping test.

Remark 5 . For the update of $(i_{t+1},j_{t+1},k_{t+1})$ in step 11, one may choose $(i,j,k)$ lexicographically among triples with the same value of $2i+j+k$ . The resulting list $\mathcal{I}$ starts with $(0,0,0),(0,0,1),(0,0,2),(0,1,1),(1,0,0),\ldots$ . A successful trial retains the current triple, while an unsuccessful trial advances to the next triple and retains the current point and residual.

Remark 7 . The first primal center is $x^{0}$ , so $\Delta_{0}$ is the original objective gap. The pair $(\hat{x},\hat{y})$ is used only as the initial point for the inner calls and is updated after each accepted trial. Algorithm 4 uses the radius bound $D_{\mathbf{y}}$ , but does not require $L_{\nabla h}$ or $\Delta_{0}$ . Its radius test cannot return failure when $D=2D_{\mathbf{y}}$ .

Remark 8 . It can be observer from the above theorem that ALgorithm 5 enjoys a $O(\epsilon^{-5/2})$ operation complexity for finding an $\epsilon$ -stationary point $(x,y)$ of ( 1 ). To the best of our knowledge, this improves the best known complexity be a logarithmic factor for the first time. Moreover, our method is parameter-free and equipped with a verifiable termination criterion.
